name: Rakshasa
description: A class of powerful supernatural beings in Hindu, Buddhist, and Jain traditions, often depicted as malevolent shape-shifting demons but including morally complex and even virtuous individuals.
full_description: Rakshasas (Sanskrit rākṣasa) are a class of supernatural beings in Indian religious and epic literature, prominently in the Ramayana and Mahabharata. They are commonly described as fierce, shape-shifting beings with two protruding fangs, sharp claw-like nails, flaming red eyes, and the ability to assume any form through māyā (illusion). Their characterizations span a wide moral range: man-eating warriors of darkness in many epic episodes, neutral or merely powerful beings in others, and morally virtuous figures such as Vibhīṣaṇa, the brother of Rāvaṇa who allies with Rāma. In Buddhist scripture, several rakshasas convert to the dharma and become protectors of Buddhist teachings. The tradition spread with Indic religion across South and Southeast Asia, where Indonesian and Malay raksasa came to mean simply 'giant'.

aliases.name: Rākṣasa
aliases.meaning: demon, fiend, that which is to be guarded against

aliases.name: Asura
aliases.meaning: broader class of power-seeking beings, sometimes overlapping

origin: Rakshasa traditions span the entire Indic cultural sphere: South Asia (India, Nepal, Sri Lanka, Bangladesh), Buddhist East Asia by way of scripture, and Southeast Asia where the loanword 'raksasa' is widely used.

etymology.origin: From Sanskrit रक्षस् (rakṣas), connected to the verbal root rakṣ- 'to guard, protect', with the noun originally referring to that which must be guarded against.
etymology.meaning: 'Demon', 'fiend', or literally 'that which is to be warded off'.
etymology.first_use: Attested in the Ṛgveda (c. 1500–1200 BCE) as rakṣas, denoting harmful spirits opposed by Agni and Indra.

timeline.event: Earliest references to rakṣas as harmful spirits in the Ṛgveda
timeline.significance: Foundational Vedic stratum of the concept

timeline.event: Composition and redaction of the Mahābhārata, including rakshasa figures such as Hiḍimba, Bakāsura, and Ghatotkaca
timeline.significance: Rakshasas as fully developed epic characters

timeline.event: Composition of the Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa, with Rāvaṇa and the rakshasas of Lankā as principal antagonists
timeline.significance: Establishes the canonical narrative of rakshasa kingdom

timeline.event: Lotus Sūtra (Saddharma Puṇḍarīka) and other Mahāyāna scriptures depict rakṣasīs as dharma-protectors after conversion
timeline.significance: Buddhist reframing of rakshasas as potential protectors

timeline.event: Indic loanword raksasa fully established in Old Javanese and Malay literatures with sense 'giant'

related.name: Yaksha

related.name: Raksasa (Indonesia/Malaysia)
related.description: Semantic shift to mean 'giant' in maritime Southeast Asia

cultural_notes: In classical Hindu cosmology, rakshasas are real ontological beings within a tiered cosmos that includes devas, asuras, yakshas, gandharvas, and other classes. Folk belief in many regions has historically associated misfortune at night with rakshasa-like spirits, addressed through mantra, amulet, and ritual.

sources.title: The Rāmāyaṇa of Vālmīki: An Epic of Ancient India (Princeton translation, 7 vols.)
